There are no known health benefits of vasectomy beyond its role in preventing pregnancy in a partner. 3. Known health risks associated with vasectomy are minimal. 4. Rare complications include severe scrotal or testicular pain that may persist for months or years. 5. Uncommon to very rare complications include infections at the incision site, which are less likely with the no-scalpel technique compared to the conventional incision method. 6. Rarely, bleeding under the skin may occur, leading to swelling or bruising (hematoma). 7. Clients should be reassured that they are welcome to return at any time if they experience problems, have questions, or if their partner suspects pregnancy. 8. A small percentage of vasectomies may fail, resulting in pregnancy. 9. Clients should seek medical attention if they experience symptoms such as bleeding, pain, pus, heat, swelling, or redness in the genital area that worsens or does not resolve. 10. General health advice includes seeking immediate medical care if a client feels something is seriously wrong with their health after the procedure. 11. Any health problem following a surgical procedure should be carefully assessed and considered related to the procedure until proven otherwise. 12. Informed decision-making is crucial. A counselor should provide clear, practical information about the procedure, including its permanence, to help clients make an informed choice. 13. Involving a partner in counseling can be helpful but is not mandatory. 14. If complications arise, providers should listen to the client’s concerns, offer advice and support, and provide treatment if necessary. 15. Female sterilization is a permanent surgical contraceptive method for women who do not wish to have more children. 16. The two most common surgical approaches are minilaparotomy and laparoscopy. 17. Minilaparotomy involves a small incision in the abdomen to access and block or cut the fallopian tubes. 18. Laparoscopy uses a thin tube with lenses inserted through a small incision to block or cut the fallopian tubes. 19. Female sterilization is also known as tubal sterilization, tubal ligation, voluntary surgical contraception, tubectomy, bi-tubal ligation, tying the tubes, minilap, or the operation. 20. The procedure works by blocking or cutting the fallopian tubes, preventing eggs from meeting sperm. 21. Female sterilization is one of the most effective contraceptive methods, with less than one pregnancy per 100 women in the first year after the procedure. 22. A small risk of pregnancy remains beyond the first year and until menopause. 23. Over ten years, about two pregnancies occur per 100 women who rely on female sterilization. 24. Effectiveness varies slightly depending on the technique used, but all methods have low pregnancy rates. 25. Fertility does not return after sterilization, as the procedure is intended to be permanent. 26. Reversal surgery is difficult, expensive, and often unavailable, and it frequently does not result in pregnancy. 27. Female sterilization does not protect against sexually transmitted infections (STIs). 28. With proper counseling and informed consent, any woman can safely undergo female sterilization, including those who are young, have no children, are breastfeeding, or are living with HIV. 29. Careful counseling is especially important in certain situations to ensure the woman does not regret her decision. 30. Female sterilization must be performed by a trained provider using either the minilaparotomy or laparoscopy procedure. 31. No woman should be denied the procedure simply because follow-up care may be difficult or unavailable. 32. Known health benefits include protection against pregnancy risks, pelvic inflammatory disease (PID), and possibly ovarian cancer, as well as a reduced risk of ectopic pregnancy. 33. Known health risks are minimal, with complications of surgery and anesthesia being uncommon to extremely rare. 34. Female sterilization is a safe method of contraception, but like other minor surgeries, it carries some risks, such as infection or wound abscess. 35. Serious complications are uncommon, and death due to the procedure or anesthesia is extremely rare. 36. The risk of complications is significantly lower with local anesthesia compared to general anesthesia. 37. Complications can be minimized with proper techniques and skilled providers in appropriate settings. 38. Clients should be reassured that they can return at any time if they experience problems, have questions, or suspect pregnancy. 39. Clients should seek medical attention if they experience symptoms such as bleeding, pain, pus, heat, swelling, or redness of the wound, high fever, fainting, persistent light-headedness, or extreme dizziness. 40. Any sudden, serious health concerns after the procedure should prompt immediate medical care. 41. A careful clinical assessment is essential before the procedure, especially in hard-to-reach areas or facilities far from higher-level health services. 42. The assessment should include a review of medical eligibility criteria and a pelvic/genital examination. 43. If complications arise, providers should listen to the client’s concerns, offer advice and support, and provide treatment if necessary. 44. Withdrawal, also known as coitus interruptus or pulling out, involves the man withdrawing his penis from the vagina before ejaculation to prevent sperm from entering the woman’s body. 45. Withdrawal is one of the least effective contraceptive methods as commonly used, with about 20 pregnancies per 100 women in the first year. 46. When used correctly with every act of sex, withdrawal results in about four pregnancies per 100 women in the first year. 47. Fertility returns immediately after stopping withdrawal. 48. Withdrawal does not protect against sexually transmitted infections (STIs). 49. All men can use withdrawal, and no medical conditions prevent its use. 50. Proper use of withdrawal requires the man to withdraw his penis before ejaculation and ensure semen does not come into contact with the woman’s external genitalia. 51. If the man has ejaculated recently, he should urinate and wash the tip of his penis before sex to remove any remaining semen. 52. Learning proper use of withdrawal may take time, and couples may benefit from using another method until the man feels confident in using withdrawal correctly. 53. Couples who have been using withdrawal effectively should not be discouraged from continuing. 54. Emergency contraceptive pills (ECPs) can be used if the man ejaculates before withdrawing. 55. Providers should explain ECP use and provide them if available.
